newsitem.title: USA: Microcredit summit meets to expand small loans.
newsitem.headline: Microcredit summit meets to expand small loans.

text.p: Alice Semosa was wearing a bright orange dress that practically shouted across the room, but her voice carried barely two feet (a meter) as she timidly described the changes in her life that began with a $40 loan.

Semosa runs a tiny grocery store in her village in South Africa and is one of 13 million poor people who have benefited from the "microcredit" movement that began in developing countries a decade ago and has reached global proportions.

This week 2,500 people from 115 countries met in Washington to set ambitious goals for helping 100 million poverty-stricken people with small loans by the year 2005, without losing the grassroots flavor.
"Microcredit gives women power," Semosa, a black South African, said through a translator. But not the power usually associated with Washington.
"Now our children are able to go to school. We are not afraid to meet people, we are just like anyone else, ordinary people," she explained proudly.

Semosa got her break from poverty in 1989 with a $40 loan from a relative to launch a clothes-selling business. After five years, she borrowed $70 from a local organization, the Small Enterprise Foundation, and began selling meat. Three years and three loans later, she runs a small grocery.
Microcredit Summit organizers brought her to Washington along with people ranging from a clothes vendor in India to an ice cream saleswoman from Bolivia to showcase their triumphs.

The idea is to help poor people who would be laughed out of a traditional bank if they tried to apply for a small loan, either because they could not fill out the application, had no collateral, or needed an amount so small that the bank would make no profit from processing the loan.

First lady Hillary Rodham Clinton, who told the conference about a "microenterprise" group in Denver, Colorado, said one woman there had told her: "Too many great ideas die in the parking lots of banks."

In some countries, these people have joined groups to guarantee each others' loans, signing with a thumbprint if they cannot write. Some of these "banks" will not give a new loan until the previous borrower pays up.
The visionary of the movement, Bangladeshi economist Mohammed Yunus, started the Grameen Bank for the poor in 1976, and found that repayment rates of loans were about 98 percent.
Yunus built an institution that caters to 1.8 million poor borrowers, lending $30 million every month.
The microcredit movement spread first to other developing nations but the Washington summit was evidence of how much attention it has attracted in the industrialized world too.

Last week President Bill Clinton announced he would request $1 billion over five years to support development of a U.S. "microenterprise development program" to increase access to credit for women, low-income people and minorities.
During the summit the Inter-American Development Bank said it planned to invest $500 million over the next five years in microenterprise development projects.

The United Nations Development Programme announced a $41 million program to improve access to small loans in developing countries. The World Bank is involved through a 1995 plan called the Consultative Group to Assist the Poorest.

But one big question is whether and how commercial banks will get involved. Conference organizers estimate up to $21.6 billion could be needed to achieve their goal of expanding credit to 100 million families by 2005.

Several commercial banks and private interests were represented at the summit. But with the exception of one Bolivian bank, none of the banks represented was involved in direct microcredit loans. Summit organizers say they are not seeking that anyway. They want the microenterprise programs -- the grassroots groups formed by entreprenuers -- to have access to capital from the commercial banks.
